I'll stop changing prompts. Three rounds moved the score 54% → 55%, which is 3 questions out of 300. The standard error at that size is about ±2.9 points, so the gain is indistinguishable from noise. **The bar.** The best published BIRD scores are about 80% execution accuracy: Gemini-SQL2 reports 80.04% on the single-model track, and Huawei DataGallery claims 82.39%. Neither is independently confirmed. Human performance on BIRD is about 93%. Our questions aren't BIRD, so I won't copy those numbers as our target. I'll provisionally aim for **≥70% on held-out**, a gain of about 15 points, which a 300-question set can detect. I'll revise that after step 2 shows how much of the gap is achievable.

1. **Protect the decision set.** All three prompt rounds were probably judged on the 300 held-out questions, so they've been partly tuned on. I'll freeze them as the final check and build a separate development set (from a new split or newly written questions) for iteration. I'll also re-run 54% vs 55% as a paired comparison on the same questions to confirm it's noise.
2. **Find what's actually failing.** I'll sort the ~135 failed questions into causes:
   - wrong or missing tables and columns (schema linking)
   - wrong literal values, e.g. `'CA'` vs `'California'`
   - join or aggregation logic
   - SQL that doesn't run
   - wrong answer keys or ambiguous questions

   - **Run-and-repair:** execute the draft query, then feed errors, empty results and sample rows back to the agent for revision.

I'll build an evaluation that predicts which descriptions reviewers will rewrite, calibrate it against their real edits, and only then use it to score the agent.

**Setting the bar.** I found no public benchmark for PR descriptions that reports how often a model judge agrees with humans. Older work scored descriptions with ROUGE against the original text ([Liu et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.06987), [Sakib et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00921v1)). That only measures word overlap. The closest example of a judge checked against humans is [SWR-Bench](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2509.01494.md), which reports about 90% agreement with people, but for code-review comments. Its approach, checking whether the output covers a list of known points, carries over to descriptions. [Qodo's PR benchmark](https://www.qodo.ai/?p=14707) uses an o3 judge but reports no human agreement. So the comparison point is your own 35% rewrite rate. Target: the judge's verdicts agree with qualified human labels at least 85% of the time on a labeled set it was never tuned on, with false passes and false failures reported separately. These labels are written from scratch, not taken from rewrites, so they also catch rewrites that were only about style. Once that holds, any agent change has to beat the incumbent on paired cases by more than the run-to-run noise.

**First steps:**
1. **Read the production path.** The agent's code isn't in this repo, so I'll start in your product repo: the entrypoint, prompt, what it reads (diff, commits, linked issue, CI), and the existing smoke test.
2. **Mine the labels.** I'll pull recent PRs and record the date range and how I picked them. For each PR I'll keep the diff, the agent's draft, and what the reviewer did: accepted, lightly edited, or rewritten. Then I'll sort the rewrites by cause, such as made-up claims, a missing reason for the change, missing risk or testing notes, wrong scope, or style only. A rewrite is a noisy label, so I'll have two qualified reviewers adjudicate a sample and keep their disagreements. I won't use the reviewer's final text as the answer key, because the diff is the source of truth.
3. **Build the cases.** Each case is a real PR with the agent run through its production entrypoint and the repository frozen at that commit. An adapter only passes inputs in and captures outputs. The labels stay hidden from the agent.

**What gets built:**
- **Code checks** for anything objective: every file, function or test the description names exists in the diff, the issue link is correct, testing claims match CI results, and no section is empty.
- **One model judge** for the meaning, which code can't check. It classifies claims against the diff as supported, unsupported or contradicted. It also checks against named criteria: motivation, behavior change, risk, and how the change was tested. It returns a structured verdict, or "cannot judge" when evidence is missing. Agent text is passed to it as data, and I'll test whether that text can steer the judge.

**Checking the evaluation before spending on it:**
- Accepted descriptions and real rewritten ones must separate by more than the variation between repeated scoring runs.
- I'll also take hand-written good descriptions and make degraded copies: one claim made up, the motivation removed, the testing notes removed. The good originals must rank above the incumbent's drafts and the copies below them.
- **Simple baselines**, run the same way: (a) commit titles pasted into the PR template; (b) one unguided model call given the diff. If either ties the agent, I'll report that as a finding about the cases. I won't make the task harder so the agent wins.
- I'll do one real agent run and keep its output, trace, tokens, cost and latency.

**Report.** Agreement with the labels, false-pass and false-fail rates with sample sizes, baseline scores, and blind spots. Possible blind spots include giant PRs, PRs with no linked issue, and how well this generalizes beyond the repositories sampled.

Sources: [Liu et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.06987), [Sakib et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00921v1), [SWR-Bench](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2509.01494.md), [Qodo](https://www.qodo.ai/?p=14707)

That rewards sounding like the human, not being accepted by reviewers. I found no published agreement figure between human raters. So I'll measure that agreement myself and treat it as the ceiling for the judge. Today the only test is a smoke test, and 35% of descriptions get rewritten. My target: on held-out PRs, the evaluation catches most of those rewrites with a measured false-pass rate. It also has to beat the simple baselines below by more than its own run-to-run noise.

1. Read the agent's production entrypoint and the smoke test: its inputs (diff, commits, linked issue, repo template), prompts, tools, and how the description gets posted. This checkout only has our skills and process docs, so I need the product repo.
2. Collect recorded runs over a stated date range. Pair what the agent wrote with what reviewers changed it to. Sort the edits by cause:
   - something false about the diff
   - a missing reason for the change, or missing risk or testing notes
   - a missing issue link or template section
   - just style

   The edited version serves as an independent label. The agent's own output is never treated as the right answer.
3. Have two reviewers label about 60 of those pairs on their own, to get our agreement rate between humans.

- **Cases:** frozen PR snapshots (diff, commits, issue, template) run through the real entrypoint, posting to a sandbox repo that can be reset. Split into a development set and a held-out decision set, with the rare but severe failures kept in.
- **Code checks:** every file, function, or test the description mentions exists in the diff. The issue link resolves. Required template sections are present and not empty.
- **Model judge, only for meaning:** checks each claim against the diff (supported, unsupported, or contradicted), and checks whether the reason and risk are stated. I'll report confusion counts and false-pass and false-fail rates.
- **Records:** model identity, errors, tokens, cost and latency for each attempt, with infrastructure failures kept separate from agent failures.

**Check before spending.** On the development set the scorer must clearly separate accepted descriptions from rewritten ones, by more than its noise. Then I'll run two simple baselines under the same conditions: commit messages filled into the template, and one unguided model call.

If a baseline ties the agent, that's a finding about the cases or the task. I won't make the task harder so the agent wins. After that I'll capture one full real attempt end to end, then extend to the rest of the cases.

**What you'll get:** case paths and commands, where the labels came from, scores with sample counts and spread, the baseline results, the judge's error rates and what decisions they support, and the blind spots. One example of a blind spot: anything a code reviewer needs that the PR snapshot doesn't contain.

rows.task: Our model judge agrees with human graders on 71% of 300 labeled answers. Make the judge good enough to gate releases.
rows.reply:
I'll treat "good enough to gate releases" as a target we set before tuning, based on the cost of the judge's mistakes. 71% agreement doesn't tell us much yet. It depends on the share of answers humans pass, and it doesn't say whether the 29% misses are false passes (bad answers that ship) or false fails (good answers that get blocked).

**First steps**
1. **Read the production path.** Trace how the release gate prepares inputs, builds the prompt, calls the judge model, parses the output and makes the decision. Calibration has to run through that same code, not a copy of the prompt.
2. **Measure the 71% properly.** Compute confusion counts for the 300 answers, false-pass and false-fail rates with denominators, cannot-judge and parse-failure counts, and Cohen's κ. Also score two trivial baselines: always "pass", and the majority class. If 71% of the labels are "pass", the judge is no better than a constant.
3. **Check the labels.** For a sample of about 60 answers, get a second qualified human label. Human-to-human agreement on our own data is the ceiling the judge can reach. For a published reference point, GPT-4 matched human preferences at over 80% agreement in MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, about the same as humans agreed with each other ([Zheng et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685)). That was pairwise preference, though, so our own human-to-human number is the real bar.
4. **Set the gate's tolerance with you before tuning.** I'll propose a bound like: false-pass rate ≤ X% (upper confidence bound, not the point estimate), false-fail ≤ Y%, and κ within a small margin of human-to-human. **This is the input I need from you: how costly is a bad release compared with a blocked good one?**

**What I'll measure, and against what**
- I'll split the 300 into about 200 for calibration and about 100 held out, stratified by label and borderline status. The held-out set is used once, for the final go/no-go.
- On the 29% where judge and humans disagree, I'll sort each case by cause: wrong label, unclear criteria, missing evidence (for example, the judge trusting the answer's own claims about what it did), prompt behaviour, or parser failure. I'll fix the cause rather than just reword the prompt.
- I'll run each case 3–5 times to measure how often the judge disagrees with itself. That decides whether the gate needs majority voting.
- Adversarial cases: answers that try to instruct the judge, and answers with evidence removed. Both must come out as fail or cannot-judge, never as a default pass.

**What I'll build**
- A judge that returns a structured verdict: a decision, a result per named criterion, evidence references, a short reason, and an explicit cannot-judge option. Malformed output fails.
- A calibration script, `scripts/judge-calibration.py`, that runs the production path over the labeled set and writes confusion tables, error rates with confidence intervals, and raw outputs to `build/judge-calibration/`. Each run is tagged with the model, prompt hash and input digest so drift can be checked later.
- A gate that blocks on any deterministic failure first, and treats cannot-judge as "needs a human", not "pass".

If no version meets the agreed tolerance on the held-out set, I'll report which kinds of decision the judge can safely gate and which it can't. I won't loosen the bar after seeing results. The work goes on a branch named `feat/judge-release-gate`, with formatting changes in a separate commit from the logic.

Sources: [Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685)

- Labeled cases for the gaps above: borderline answers, fluent failures, missing or irrelevant evidence, and injection attempts.
- A gate rule: block on a judged fail, and send "cannot judge" cases to a person. A judge score never overrides a failed deterministic check.

   - a confusion matrix, with false-pass and false-fail rates and their denominators;
   - how often the judge returns cannot-judge, and how often the parser fails;
   - which raw outputs disagree with their parsed decisions.

**Setting the bar**
- **Best known design.** [Orb](https://docs.withorb.com/architecture/query-based-billing) computes each metric fresh from raw events when it makes an invoice, and applies corrections as a layer when reading, so every consumer sees one answer. [Stripe meters](https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/recording-usage-api) drop repeat events that share an identifier. Two caveats: Stripe processes usage in the background, so totals can lag, and I haven't confirmed the full list of Stripe's aggregation functions.
- **Our number.** Four implementations disagree by up to 3% on the same customer-month. How often they disagree, and in which direction, is unmeasured.
- **Target.** One implementation, and zero difference between invoice, dashboard, usage alerts and finance export, apart from documented late-arriving events.
- **Check.** Recompute every customer-month from the last 12 months with the new module and compare it with what was actually invoiced. Every difference must be explained by a named cause. The three old paths must be deleted.

**First steps**
1. Find the four implementations and write down, for each, its source table, how it cuts off the month (UTC or account timezone), how it removes duplicates, what it does with late events, how it rounds, and what it filters out.
2. Run all four on the same customer-months and sort each difference by which of those causes produced it. That turns "up to 3%" into a measured breakdown, and tells us which behaviour is correct, which is a decision for the billing owner.
3. Agree the vocabulary in a new `CONTEXT.md`:
   - **Usage event:** an immutable raw record carrying an idempotency key.
   - **Meter:** an event filter plus an aggregation.
   - **Billing period:** a span of time in the account's timezone.
   - **Metered quantity:** the result of a meter over a period, as of a point in time.
   - Terms to avoid: "usage" on its own, and "consumption".

**Interface options**
- **A. One function:** `meter(customer, meterId, period, asOf) → Quantity`. Callers can't drift because they have nothing to configure.
- **B. Query builder:** callers can combine filters and windows freely. This is flexible, but it lets them recreate four different answers.
- **C. Precomputed table:** the module writes period totals that callers read. Reads are fast, but the stored totals go stale whenever corrections arrive.
- **D. Ports and adapters:** A with a swappable event store, Postgres in production and PGlite in tests. It's justified because production and tests really do use different backends.

**My recommendation is A over D.** Removing duplicates, assigning events to periods, applying corrections, and rounding (only once, at the end) all happen inside, behind one small interface. Passing `asOf` keeps past invoices reproducible after late events or corrections arrive. If a cache is ever needed, it goes behind the same interface. Deleting this module would push the complexity back into four callers, so it earns its place.

- The reconciliation script from step 2, which serves as the check before and after the change.

rows.reply:
I'll start by measuring the 3% before designing anything, because the causes of the disagreement determine the interface. The plan is one deep module that holds every metering rule and replaces all four implementations.

**The bar**
- **Best known design:** Orb treats billing as a replayable calculation over an immutable event log, kept separate from ingestion. Stripe meters and OpenMeter give each meter one aggregation definition and deduplicate on a stable event ID (OpenMeter uses CloudEvents id plus source). Mostly vendor sources; I couldn't confirm Stripe's dedup window in Stripe's own docs.
- **Our number:** four implementations, up to 3% apart on the same customer-month. I don't yet know what share of customer-months disagree, the dollar impact, or which defects come from the split. Measuring that is step 1.
- **Target:** 0 disagreements. With one implementation, two callers can't differ unless the code is nondeterministic. Every invoice line can be reproduced from the event log, and 4 implementations become 1.
- **Check:** recompute the last 6 months of customer-months and compare against the invoices already issued. Pass: every number matches exactly, or each gap is explained by a defect we fix on purpose. Done when all four callers are migrated and the old code is deleted.

**First steps**
1. Find the four places usage is computed and the callers of each. I'll write down how each one handles dedup keys, period boundaries (timezone, inclusive or exclusive end), late events, rounding (float vs decimal), and filters.
2. Run all four on the same sample of customer-months and record, per case, how far they disagree and which rule caused it. That's the measured cost.
3. Read `CONTEXT.md` and the ADRs in the product repo. This skills repo has none. I'll settle the terms: "usage event", "meter", "billing period", "usage total". I'd avoid "consumption", "metrics" and "counts".

**The interface (recommended)**
```
meter(definition: MeterDefinition, customer, period: BillingPeriod, events: UsageEventSource) -> UsageTotal
```
It's a pure function. Dedup on event ID, period boundaries in UTC, late-event and correction rules, decimal rounding, and aggregation (sum, max or last) all live inside it. `UsageTotal` includes the IDs of the events counted, so any invoice line can be explained.

**The one seam:** `UsageEventSource`. The production adapter reads Postgres, and tests run against PGlite with the same adapter code, with no mocks. That makes two real adapters, which justifies the seam. I'll add no other ports.

**Options I'm rejecting**
- A shared helper library: the four callers would keep their own boundary logic, so they'd keep drifting.
- A streaming aggregator that fixes totals when events arrive: totals can't be recomputed after a correction.
- A configurable rules engine: it adds interface without adding depth.

**What I'll build**
- The module, written test-first (`/tdd`), with tests only through `meter()`. The tests cover duplicate events, events exactly at a period boundary, late events, and leap or DST months.
- A replay harness that runs the module and each old implementation over the historical sample.
- I'll migrate callers one at a time, watching the replay diff each time, then delete the four implementations and their tests (`/simplify`).

**Decisions for you**
- If the replay shows customers were over- or under-billed, adopting the correct rule changes their invoices. You or finance decide that, not me.
- I'll write an ADR for "usage is always recomputed from the immutable event log and never stored as running totals." That choice is hard to undo.

Finally, I'll log the run: `skill-run-log /codebase-design --target "billing usage metering" --verdict PARTIAL --next /tdd`.
